title: Analyzing Uncertainty of LLM -as-a-Judge: Interval Evaluations with Conformal Prediction
robustness_types: LLM judge model choice; prompting strategy; judge framework; calibration-data size; judge reprompting; task/dataset variation
explicit_limitations: The study primarily covers summarization and reasoning for natural language generation using rating-based evaluations. evidence_summary: The paper does not name or evaluate any languages, but explicitly limits its task coverage and notes that machine translation and multimodal generation remain unexplored, providing partial support for a multilingual reliability gap. It tests several robustness-related factors—judge model, prompting strategy, judge framework, calibration-set size, datasets, and reprompting—but does not establish comprehensive robustness across all perturbations such as ordering, repeated generations, or broader domain shifts. It also compares judge outputs with human annotations and evaluates bias using MSE, MAE, and correlation.

explicit_limitations: The paper identifies rapid saturation and possible reward hacking when judge capabilities are not improved. evidence_summary: The study does not explicitly name or evaluate any languages, so it provides no direct multilingual evidence. It does test several robustness-related issues: positional bias through reordered judgment comparisons, length bias through a length-control mechanism, and score bias in meta-judge analyses. However, it does not provide a broad evaluation across prompt wording, languages, domains, models, or repeated-run conditions.

title: Self-Augmented Preference Alignment for Sycophancy Reduction in LLM s
explicit_limitations: Performance under the negated suggestion template was less consistent, which the authors attribute to a conflict between sycophancy and handling negation. They also state that Falcon-7B's weaker ability to learn preferences limited the effect of SAA.
evidence_summary: The paper evaluates multiple open-source models on Answer Suggestion and Are You Sure tasks and compares several suggestion prompt templates, including correct, incorrect, and negated suggestions. title: Beyond the Score: Uncertainty-Calibrated LLM s for Automated Essay Assessment
robustness_types: corpus/domain variation; model variation; label-space variation; prompt-style variation; proficiency-level variation
explicit_limitations: The study is confined to English and three public essay corpora. The conformal guarantee relies on calibration and test data being exchangeable; topic drift, candidate demographics, or language-transfer effects in real exam sessions could weaken reliability. The study also notes that calibrated sets indicate confidence but do not explain why an essay receives a particular score.
explicit_future_work: The authors plan to study model-size scaling from 1B to 13B across several model families, test finer-grained FCE bands and ordinal-aware conformal scores, use rubric-aware prompting conditioned on essay characteristics, conduct a teacher-in-the-loop study, and pursue broader user studies.
evidence_summary: The paper explicitly limits evaluation to English, providing direct evidence consistent with a multilingual reliability gap. It evaluates several corpora, models, rubric sizes, prompt styles, and proficiency levels, but does not systematically test prompt wording, repeated runs, ordering effects, judge bias, or broader perturbation stability. The authors explicitly identify topic drift, demographics, and language-transfer effects as risks to reliability.

evidence_summary: The evaluation uses an English-language poetry dataset and reports no multilingual or low-resource-language experiments.
